\chapter{Four Things Outdoors --- Wind, Snow, Tree, Flower}
\label{ch:al-aire-libre}
\hlchaptermodality{278}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the wind, the snow, a tree and a flower in Spanish, and say for each whether its English relative is an inherited cousin or a later borrowing.}

Complete ES-C278-flor: say all four words, then sort their English relatives into cousins and loans.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el viento]{el viento — a word English happens to own twice}

\label{lesson:ES-C278-viento}



\begin{quote}
You have just spent a long run of lessons on words for arguing, citing and summarising. What follows is the opposite kind of material: plain, solid things you can point at.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el tiempo — the weather, and the word for it.
  \item hace calor, hace frío, hace sol — saying what the weather is doing today.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{VIEN-to}, stress on the first syllable. The \emph{ie} is the same opening-out you have met before in \emph{quiero} and \emph{tiene}: one Latin vowel arriving in Spanish as two. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el viento} — \textquotedblleft{}the wind.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{ventus}, with its short stressed \emph{e} opening into \emph{ie} on the road into Spanish. That single change is why the vowel you say is not the vowel Latin wrote.

The interesting part is on the English side. \textbf{Wind} was not taken from \emph{ventus}. The two words go back to one much older ancestor and came down two separate family lines, which is why they resemble each other only faintly. \textbf{Ventilate} and \textbf{vent}, by contrast, \emph{are} Latin \emph{ventus}, carried into English out of books long after English already had a perfectly good word for moving air.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A cousin and a loan leave different marks, and you can often see which you are holding.

An inherited word has been in the mouth for two thousand years, and each language has worn it down its own way — one ancestor came out as \emph{viento} here and as \emph{wind} there. A borrowed word arrives late, in writing, and stays tidy: \emph{ventilate} still looks Latin because it has had almost no time to stop looking Latin.

Keep that test. It will pay off in nearly every word ahead.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el viento}
  \item which English word is the cousin and which is the loan (\emph{wind}; \emph{ventilate})
  \item one sentence about the weather with \emph{hace}, and one with \emph{el viento}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word stands behind \emph{viento}? (\emph{Ventus}.) Is English \emph{wind} borrowed from it? (No — a cousin, down a separate line from the same ancestor.) Which English word is the actual loan? (\emph{Ventilate}, or \emph{vent}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la nieve]{la nieve — the same vowel trick, and a missing s}

\label{lesson:ES-C278-nieve}



\begin{quote}
You have one weather word already. Here is a second, and it repeats the sound change you just met — which is how you will start to recognise it on your own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el viento — the wind, and the \emph{ie} that came out of a Latin \emph{e}.
  \item llueve — saying that it is raining.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{NIE-ve}, stress on the first syllable, and the \emph{v} said with the lips barely meeting — the soft \emph{b} sound you already use in \emph{vino}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la nieve} — \textquotedblleft{}the snow.\textquotedblright{}

Latin's word was \textbf{nix}, but its other forms carry the stem \emph{niv-}, and it is that stem — through the form \emph{nivem} — that Spanish grew from. The short stressed \emph{e} opened into \emph{ie}, exactly as it did a moment ago, and \emph{nivem} came out as \emph{nieve}.

English \textbf{snow} is the cousin. The shared ancestor began with an \emph{s} that Latin dropped and the Germanic side kept, so the two words differ at the front and agree behind it. Latin's own form does reach English, but only in cold technical corners: \textbf{niveous} for snow-white, and the \emph{nival} zone near the top of a mountain.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Twice now, a Latin \emph{e} under stress has arrived in Spanish as \emph{ie}. That is no longer a fact about one word; it is a pattern you can carry.

When you meet a Spanish word with \emph{ie} whose Latin or English relative shows a plain \emph{e}, you are almost certainly looking at this same event, two thousand years old, still visible in the spelling.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la nieve}, then \emph{el viento}
  \item the Latin stem behind it (\emph{niv-})
  \item what English kept at the front of \emph{snow} that Latin threw away
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which sound change turned \emph{nivem} into \emph{nieve}? (Stressed \emph{e} opening into \emph{ie} — the same one behind \emph{viento}.) What separates \emph{nieve} from English \emph{snow} at the very front? (An \emph{s} the Latin line lost.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el árbol]{el árbol — one letter away from Latin}

\label{lesson:ES-C278-arbol}



\begin{quote}
Some words changed a great deal on the way from Latin. This one changed by a single letter, and the letter it changed tells you something about mouths rather than about Spanish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item verde — green, from a Latin verb meaning to flourish.
  \item á é í ó ú — what a written accent does to the stress.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ÁR-bol}. The accent is written because the stress falls on the first syllable while the word ends in \emph{l}, which is not where the default would put it. The \emph{r} is a single tap, not a roll. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el árbol} — \textquotedblleft{}the tree.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{arbor}, and Spanish kept nearly all of it. What moved is the second \emph{r}, which became \emph{l}.

Two \emph{r} sounds a syllable apart are awkward to keep distinct, and a tongue that says the word ten thousand times will look for a way out. Spanish took it. Portuguese, next door, did not: its tree is \emph{árvore}, both \emph{r} sounds intact. The escape route was available, not compulsory, and that is worth knowing before you start expecting sound changes to be laws.

English holds the Latin word too, untouched: \textbf{arbor}, \textbf{arboreal}, \textbf{arboretum}. Both \emph{r} sounds still there, because a word borrowed out of a book escapes everything an inherited word lives through.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
This is the cousin-and-loan test again, from the other direction.

\emph{Árbol} is the inherited form, and it carries a scar: one sound gave way to another for no reason except ease. \emph{Arboretum} is the loan, and it carries no scar at all. When two English words look like a Spanish one but only the tidy one matches it letter for letter, the tidy one is usually the late arrival.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el árbol}, stressing the first syllable
  \item the Latin word, and which of its letters moved (\emph{arbor}; the second \emph{r})
  \item \emph{el viento, la nieve, el árbol} — the three you now have
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What single change separates \emph{árbol} from \emph{arbor}? (The second \emph{r} became \emph{l}.) Did every Romance language make it? (No — Portuguese kept \emph{árvore}.) Why does English \emph{arboretum} look more Latin than the Spanish word does? (It was borrowed late, not inherited.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la flor]{la flor — and the English word hiding inside your bread}

\label{lesson:ES-C278-flor}



\begin{quote}
The last of the four outdoor words, and the one with the best surprise waiting on the English side.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el árbol — the tree, one letter from Latin.
  \item el pan — bread, which this lesson comes back to.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{flor}, one syllable, ending in a single tapped \emph{r}. Spanish does not put a vowel into the \emph{fl-} cluster, so it starts cleanly. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la flor} — \textquotedblleft{}the flower.\textquotedblright{}

Latin's bare form was \textbf{flos}, but its other forms show the stem \emph{flor-}, and Spanish built on the stem, as it did with \emph{nieve}. Feminine, so \emph{la flor}, even though the ending gives you no help at all.

English took the same stem twice. Once through French, as \textbf{flower}. And once — this is the surprise — as \textbf{flour}. The finest part of ground grain, sifted out from the rest, was called the \emph{flower} of the meal, in the sense of \emph{the best of it}. For centuries English wrote both senses the same way, and only later split the spelling so that a baker and a gardener could stop confusing each other.

\textbf{Flourish}, \textbf{floral} and \textbf{flora} are the same root again, arriving in more obviously Latin clothes.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You now have four ordinary outdoor words, and each one taught a different way a word can travel.

\emph{Viento} showed a cousin beside a loan. \emph{Nieve} showed a sound change repeating, so you could recognise it rather than memorise it. \emph{Árbol} showed a change that one language made and its neighbour did not. And \emph{flor} shows a single word splitting in two inside English, until the two halves no longer look related.

That is four kinds of movement, and none of them is Spanish being irregular. It is what happens to any word that stays in use long enough.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la flor}, with a clean \emph{fl-}
  \item what \emph{flour} originally meant (the flower, the finest part, of the ground grain)
  \item all four — \emph{el viento, la nieve, el árbol, la flor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin stem gave \emph{flor}? (\emph{Flor-}, from \emph{flos}.) Which everyday English word is the same word as \emph{flower}? (\emph{Flour}.) Is \emph{la flor} masculine or feminine? (Feminine, and its ending tells you nothing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
